questions.q: How does a scalability question differ from a performance question, as this lesson defines them?
options: They are exactly the same question asked in different words
Performance asks whether code behaves well right now; scalability asks whether that same code will keep behaving well as data volume, users, and automation complexity grow over time
Scalability only applies to Batch Apex, while performance only applies to triggers
Performance is a client-side concern, while scalability is purely a database administration concern
questions.explain: Performance is about current behavior; scalability is specifically about whether that behavior holds up as the org grows, which is a forward-looking, distinct question.

options: A very large number of records owned by a single user or queue, making sharing recalculation disproportionately expensive for that owner
A bug where record ownership changes randomly without user action
A governor limit on the total number of record owners an org can have
A type of SOQL query that filters on the OwnerId field
questions.explain: Ownership skew specifically refers to an uneven concentration of records under one owner or queue, which makes sharing recalculation for that owner's huge record set disproportionately costly.

questions.q: Why might a query that is comfortably selective today stop being selective purely from data growth, with no code changes?
options: Because SOQL selectivity rules change automatically every time Salesforce releases a new version
Because selectivity is unrelated to table size and depends only on the query's syntax

Because selectivity thresholds (from Lesson 4) are based on what fraction of the table a filter matches, so the same filter matches a smaller fraction as the table grows, or a larger one if the matching subset also grows disproportionately
Because indexes automatically expire after a fixed number of records are added
questions.explain: Selectivity thresholds are expressed as a fraction (or capped count) of total table rows, so the exact same filter's selectivity can shift purely from the table growing — a scalability concern layered directly on top of Lesson 4's query optimization material.

questions.q: Why isn't "it worked fine in the sandbox" good evidence that a design will scale in production?
options: Because sandboxes always run a different Apex runtime version than production
Because sandbox governor limits are permanently fixed at zero
Because Salesforce disables all automation in sandboxes by default

Because data skew problems (ownership skew, lookup skew, related record-locking) are volume-and-distribution problems that typically don't appear in a small sandbox with a few hundred evenly-spread test records
questions.explain: Skew-driven problems depend on uneven, large-scale distribution of records, which a small, evenly-populated sandbox typically doesn't reproduce — so passing sandbox testing says little about production-scale behavior.

questions.q: What is one concrete design habit this lesson recommends to avoid creating data skew as an org grows?
options: Always disable sharing rules to prevent sharing recalculation entirely
Avoid designs that concentrate records on a single "catch-all" parent or owner by construction, such as one default Account or one default Queue absorbing an ever-growing number of child records
Store all child records directly on the User object instead of using lookups
Convert every lookup relationship into a master-detail relationship
questions.explain: A well-intentioned "default" or "catch-all" record is a common, direct cause of ownership or lookup skew, since it accumulates an ever-growing, concentrated set of child records as volume increases.
